options.text: Clearing trees across a large area, usually for farming or building
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The natural fall of dead leaves
options.explanation: Leaf fall is natural; deforestation clears whole forest stands.
Planting adds trees; deforestation removes them.
Grassland drying is not tree clearing.

questions.stem: Why does leaching rise after trees are felled?

options.explanation: Acidity is not the stated mechanism.

options.text: No roots take up the soil minerals, so rain washes them into nearby water
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Rain continues; uptake is what stops.
Minerals are washed away, not multiplied.

questions.stem: What holds soil in place inside a healthy forest?

options.explanation: Fungi help, but roots plus organic matter are the named anchors.
Rock lies below the soil; it does not bind the surface.

options.text: Tree roots together with organic matter
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Wind actually exposes bare soil once trees fall.

questions.stem: How does felling trees disturb the water cycle?

options.text: Trees store all rain in trunks
options.explanation: Trunks do not bank rainfall; transpiration is the pathway.
The effect works through reduced vapour, not instant loss.
No such permanent change is described.

options.text: Reduced transpiration releases less water vapour, so cloud formation and rainfall fall
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Why does deforestation add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere twice over?

options.text: Less photosynthesis removes less carbon dioxide, and burning felled trees releases more
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Trees exhale carbon dioxide when alive
options.explanation: Living trees absorb it during photosynthesis.
The named route is carbon dioxide via photosynthesis loss and combustion.
Fermentation is not the documented mechanism.

questions.stem: State the term for soil being washed and blown away after tree removal.
questions.modelAnswer: Soil erosion is the term for soil being washed or blown away once roots and organic matter no longer hold it.

questions.stem: Name the process by which trees release water vapour into the air.
questions.modelAnswer: Transpiration is the process by which trees release water vapour into the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Explain why cleared forest land loses fertility quickly.
questions.modelAnswer: Cleared land loses fertility because leaching washes away soil minerals and erosion strips the soil itself, leaving little for new growth.

questions.stem: A logging company burns its felled timber on site. State two atmospheric effects.
questions.modelAnswer: The burning releases carbon dioxide by combustion, and with fewer trees standing, less carbon dioxide is removed by photosynthesis.
